newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Activists vow to disrupt Taiwan nuclear debate.
newsitem.headline: Activists vow to disrupt Taiwan nuclear debate.

text.p: Anti-nuclear groups and opposition lawmakers vowed on Monday to disrupt parliament's review of Taiwan's controversial fourth nuclear power station, ensuring a new flare-up in a high-stakes dispute with the government.
Hanging in the balance is a US$1.8 billion contract awarded to U.S. giant General Electric to supply the twin-reactor power plant's core components.

Parliament on May 24 dealt an embarrassing blow to Taipei's nuclear energy policy, halting the 2,700-megawatt plant's US$4.1 billion budget on the very day of Taiwan Power Co's final tender for the facility's two reactors.
The cabinet formally appealed against the cancellation on June 6 but can be thwarted by a two-thirds vote of parliament.
Parliament was scheduled to debate the appeal on Tuesday.

Analysts were reluctant to say whether opponents could muster the votes necessary to make the cancellation stand, a move that experts said would be equivalent to a no-confidence vote with grave implications for Premier Lien Chan.
Both sides were preparing for what could be a dramatic showdown.
A dozen environmental activists began a sit-in on Monday outside parliament and said protests would continue through Friday when deputies vote on a final ruling.
"There will be a large-scale anti-nuclear demonstration tomorrow (Tuesday)," a spokesman for Taiwan's main opposition Democratic Progressive Party told Reuters.
"Our position is firm and clear -- we will do everything we can to reject the project again," the spokesman said.
Opposition lawmakers planned to block all entrances to prevent Premier Lien from entering to address parliament about the project, the opposition spokesman said.
The state-funded Central News Agency said the ruling Nationalist Party's legislative caucus was mobilising its allies in parliament to ensure the nuclear project's approval.
Taipower, which has continued with work despite the deadlock and considers the project alive unless a final rejection is approved, asked General Electric in September to start work.
General Electric, whose contract can be annulled if funding is not restored, declined to comment on the project.
Taipower already has poured more than US$220 million into the plant's construction at Kungliao, north of Taipei.
Taiwan approved the plant in 1994 after years of delays and protests triggered mainly by the 1986 Chernobyl nuclear disaster in the then Soviet Union.

Taipower produces 21,900 megawatts of power a year, about 23.5 percent of which is generated by nuclear plants. Experts say total output must rise to 36,000 megawatts by 2002 to keep pace with Taiwan's economic growth.
A growing number of opponents in increasingly democratic Taiwan say nuclear power is dangerous and unnecessary if alternative energy sources are pursued.
Taipower insists the nuclear plant is environmentally sound and safe, designed to the world's most advanced standards.
